a: As for this house, high as it is, everyone
t: High, or a heap of ruins?
p: The Hebrew says this house 'will be high.' Many scholars correct it to 'will become a ruin.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); compare 2 Chronicles 7:21, 'which was high'
readings.en: and this house will be high (exalted)
readings.plain: As for this house, high as it is, everyone

readings.w: Old Latin and Syriac (Peshitta), as usually read; scholarly emendation לְעִיִּין (le'iyyin); followed by NRSV, ESV, NIV
readings.en: this house will become heaps of ruins
readings.plain: This house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone

why: The Hebrew makes sense as it stands if read as a concession: the temple is lofty now, but people will be shocked at what happens to it. 2 Chronicles 7:21 supports the word 'high.' The emendation is attractive and may be right, since a word for 'ruins' (iyyim) looks much like 'high' (elyon) in Hebrew letters, but it has no direct support in a Hebrew manuscript.
b: Some scholars think a scribe deliberately softened a prediction of the temple's ruin. If the reader switches, the verse reads: 'This house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone who passes by it will be stunned...' (Micah 3:12 uses iyyim of Jerusalem in ruins).

a: Tamar
p: The written Hebrew says Tamar, a town in the south. The reading tradition and Chronicles say Tadmor (Palmyra) in Syria.

readings.en: Tamar
readings.plain: Tamar

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (the reading tradition); 2 Chronicles 8:4; Targum; Vulgate; KJV
readings.en: Tadmor
readings.plain: Tadmor

why: Every other town in 9:17–18 lies in the south and west of Israel, guarding roads, and 'in the wilderness, in the land' fits the Negev. Tamar appears as a southern border point in Ezekiel 47:19 and 48:28. The Qere follows Chronicles, which places Solomon's building in Syria (2 Chronicles 8:3–4). Most modern scholars and the BSB prefer Tamar.
b: Tadmor is the oasis city later called Palmyra, deep in the Syrian desert. Chronicles' reading enlarges Solomon's realm toward the Euphrates. A fortress at Ein Hatseva in the Arabah has been suggested for Tamar.

a: four hundred and twenty talents
p: The Hebrew of Kings has 420 talents, Chronicles 450, and the Greek 120.

readings.en: four hundred and twenty talents
readings.plain: four hundred and twenty talents

readings.en: four hundred and fifty talents
readings.plain: four hundred and fifty talents

readings.w: Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus (which also spells the place Sophira)
readings.en: a hundred and twenty talents
readings.plain: a hundred and twenty talents

why: Numbers are easily miscopied, and none of the three can be shown to be original. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew of Kings. The Greek figure matches Hiram's payment in 9:14 and the queen of Sheba's gift in 10:10 (a hundred and twenty talents each), which may have influenced it; Chronicles' 450 may be a copying slip or a rounding.

a: Your men are fortunate!
p: The Hebrew says 'your men.' The Greek and Syriac say 'your wives,' a difference of one letter.

readings.en: your men
readings.plain: Your men are fortunate!

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus and others, hai gynaikes sou); Syriac Peshitta; followed by RSV, NRSV
readings.en: your wives
readings.plain: Your wives are fortunate!

why: 'Your men' is the reading of the Hebrew in both Kings and Chronicles, and it pairs naturally with 'your servants.' The Greek reading may come from reading the Hebrew without its first letter (nasheka 'your wives' for anasheka 'your men'), or it may be original, since a queen might well mention the king's wives.

a: the throne had a round top
t: A round top, or a calf's head?
p: The Hebrew says the throne had 'a round head' behind. The Greek says 'heads of calves.'

readings.en: and the throne had a round top behind it
readings.plain: the throne had a round top

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus: protomai moschon); compare 2 Chronicles 9:18, 'a footstool of gold'
readings.en: the foreparts (heads) of calves
readings.plain: the throne had a calf's head

why: The Hebrew makes sense and is followed by most translations. But the same consonants, 'gl, can be read 'agol (round) or 'egel (calf), and some scholars think the Masoretes chose 'round' to avoid a calf image on Solomon's throne, given Jeroboam's calves (12:28). Bull and calf images on royal furniture are well attested in the region, so the Greek may preserve the older reading.

a: gold and silver, ivory, monkeys and apes
t: Ivory and monkeys, or carved stones?
p: The oldest Greek lists a different cargo: gold and silver, and carved and hewn stones, with no ivory and no animals.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; 2 Chronicles 9:21; Targum; Vulgate; KJV ('apes, and peacocks')
readings.en: gold and silver, ivory, apes and (peacocks or baboons)
readings.plain: gold and silver, ivory, monkeys and apes

readings.orig: χρυσίου καὶ ἀργυρίου καὶ λίθων τορευτῶν καὶ πελεκητῶν
readings.en: gold and silver, and carved stones and hewn stones
readings.plain: gold and silver, carved stones and hewn stones

why: The Hebrew is supported by Chronicles. Its three rare loanwords (ivory, two kinds of monkey) are the kind of words a translator might not know, and the Greek may have replaced them with a guess, perhaps drawn from the cut stone of the temple building (5:17). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: See the note on 'monkeys and apes' for the meaning of the animal words, which disappear altogether in the Greek.

a: he was king over Aram
p: The Hebrew says Rezon ruled Aram. The Greek makes this verse end Hadad's story: he ruled in Edom.

readings.en: and he reigned over Aram
readings.plain: he was king over Aram

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus), which also places the end of Hadad's story here
readings.en: and he reigned in the land of Edom
readings.plain: he was king over Edom

why: In the Hebrew the verse is about Rezon of Damascus, and 'Aram' fits. The words Aram and Edom differ in Hebrew only by the letters r and d, which look almost alike, so a slip in either direction is easy. The Greek arrangement, which has Hadad return to his land (after 11:22) and rule Edom, is smoother, and some scholars think it is older; others think the Greek translator tidied a difficult Hebrew paragraph.

a: One tribe will stay his
p: The Hebrew says one tribe will stay with Solomon's house. The Greek says two. Goes with the variant at 11:36.

readings.en: and the one tribe shall be his
readings.plain: One tribe will stay his

readings.en: and two tribes (sceptres) shall be his
readings.plain: Two tribes will stay his

why: The Hebrew 'one' leaves the sum ten plus one, which is why interpreters have long asked where the twelfth tribe went (see the note at 11:13). The Greek 'two' makes the sum twelve and fits 12:21, where Rehoboam musters Judah and Benjamin. That smoothness is a reason to suspect the Greek of correcting the arithmetic; the harder Hebrew reading is kept.

a: This is because they left me. They bowed down
p: The Hebrew blames 'they' (the people). The Greek, Syriac and Latin blame 'he' (Solomon), and the Greek keeps the singular through the whole verse ('he did not walk in my ways'); switching here changes only the first two clauses.

readings.en: because they have forsaken me and bowed down
readings.plain: This is because they left me. They bowed down

readings.en: because he has forsaken me and worshiped
readings.plain: This is because he left me. He bowed down

why: The plural is the harder reading, and the versions may have smoothed it to match the context, which is about Solomon (11:31–34). The plural may mean Solomon and his wives, or the people who followed him. The verse ends with 'like his father David,' which shows Solomon is in view either way.

a: His son will get one tribe from me
p: Goes with the variant at 11:32: the Greek again has two tribes.

readings.en: and to his son I will give one tribe
readings.plain: His son will get one tribe from me

readings.orig: τῷ δὲ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ δώσω τὰ δύο σκῆπτρα
readings.en: and to his son I will give the two tribes
readings.plain: His son will get two tribes from me

why: As at 11:32, the Hebrew 'one' is the harder reading and is kept. The Greek count of two matches Judah plus Benjamin (12:21; compare the Greek at 12:20).

a: For this I will bring David's line low, though not for all time.'"
t: A verse missing from the Greek
p: The oldest Greek text does not have 11:39, the promise that David's line will not be humbled forever.

readings.orig: וַאֲעַנֶּה אֶת־זֶרַע דָּוִד לְמַעַן זֹאת אַךְ לֹא כָל־הַיָּמִים
readings.en: And I will afflict the offspring of David for this, but not forever
readings.plain: For this I will bring David's line low, though not for all time.'"

readings.en: (the verse is absent)

why: The Hebrew is well attested and the verse fits the promise to David in 11:36. Many critical scholars think it is a late addition, perhaps from the exile or after, expressing hope for the restoration of David's house; the Greek would then preserve the shorter, earlier text. The Plain English Translation keeps it with the Hebrew.

a: When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard of it, he was still in Egypt. He had run away there from King Solomon, and Jeroboam was living in Egypt.
t: Living in Egypt, or back from Egypt?
p: The Hebrew says Jeroboam 'stayed in Egypt.' Chronicles says he 'returned from Egypt.' The oldest Greek lacks the whole verse here. Goes with the variants at 12:3 and 12:12.

readings.en: and Jeroboam dwelt in Egypt
readings.plain: When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard of it, he was still in Egypt. He had run away there from King Solomon, and Jeroboam was living in Egypt.

readings.w: 2 Chronicles 10:2 (the same consonants read with other vowels, vayyashov)
readings.en: and Jeroboam returned from Egypt
readings.plain: When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard of it, he was still in Egypt. He had run away there from King Solomon, and Jeroboam came back from Egypt.

readings.w: Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus: lacks 12:2–3a here; it reports Jeroboam's return after 11:43
readings.en: (the clause is absent)

why: The consonants of 'lived' and 'returned' are the same (wyšb); the Masoretes read 'lived,' Chronicles 'returned.' The Hebrew of Kings, read as it stands, says he was still living in Egypt when he heard, and the next verse has him summoned. The Old Greek's arrangement, in which Jeroboam is not at Shechem at all until 12:20, avoids a tension with 12:20 ('Jeroboam had returned').
b: See the variant at 12:3, which goes with this one.

a: So they sent for him and called him, and Jeroboam came with the whole assembly of Israel. They said to Rehoboam,
p: Goes with the variants at 12:2 and 12:12. In the oldest Greek the people, without Jeroboam, speak to Rehoboam.

readings.orig: וַיִּשְׁלְחוּ וַיִּקְרְאוּ־לוֹ וַיָּבֹא יָרָבְעָם וְכָל־קְהַל יִשְׂרָאֵל
readings.en: and they sent and called him, and Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came
readings.plain: So they sent for him and called him, and Jeroboam came with the whole assembly of Israel. They said to Rehoboam,

readings.orig: καὶ ἐλάλησεν ὁ λαὸς πρὸς τὸν βασιλέα Ροβοαμ
readings.en: and the people spoke to King Rehoboam
readings.plain: The people spoke to King Rehoboam:

why: The Hebrew, supported by Chronicles, puts Jeroboam at the head of the northern delegation, and 12:12 mentions him again (see the variant there). But 12:20 says Israel heard 'that Jeroboam had returned' and only then called him, which fits the Greek better. Many scholars think Jeroboam's name was added at 12:2–3 and 12:12 to make him the leader of the revolt from the start; others think the Greek translator removed the tension.

a: Jeroboam and all the people
t: Did Jeroboam come back with them?
p: Goes with the variants at 12:2 and 12:3. The Greek says 'all Israel' came, without naming Jeroboam.

readings.en: Jeroboam and all the people
readings.plain: Jeroboam and all the people

readings.en: all Israel
readings.plain: all Israel

why: This is the third place (with 12:2–3) where the Hebrew names Jeroboam at Shechem and the Old Greek does not. The Greek version agrees with 12:20, where Israel sends for Jeroboam only after the assembly breaks up. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and Chronicles; see the variant at 12:3 for the two explanations.

a: except the tribe of Judah alone
t: Judah alone, or Judah and Benjamin?
p: The Hebrew says only Judah stayed with David's house. The Greek says Judah and Benjamin.

readings.en: except the tribe of Judah only
readings.plain: except the tribe of Judah alone

readings.orig: πλὴν σκήπτρου Ιουδα καὶ Βενιαμιν μόνοι
readings.en: except the tribe of Judah and Benjamin only
readings.plain: except the tribe of Judah and Benjamin alone

why: The Hebrew 'Judah alone' agrees with the 'one tribe' of 11:13, 32 and 36; the very next verse (12:21) then has Rehoboam call up Judah and Benjamin. The Greek brings this verse into line with 12:21, as it does at 11:32 and 11:36. The harder Hebrew reading is kept; the note at 11:13 gives the ways interpreters count the tribes.

a: as the LORD had said
t: The Greek's second story of Jeroboam (12:24a–z)
p: After this verse the Greek adds some 25 verses that tell Jeroboam's rise again. See the note on this verse and the chapter page.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Targum; Vulgate; KJV, NIV, ESV
readings.en: according to the word of the LORD
readings.plain: as the LORD had said

readings.w: Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus and most Greek manuscripts (Rahlfs' 3 Kingdoms 12:24a–z)
readings.orig: κατὰ τὸ ῥῆμα κυρίου ... Καὶ ἄνθρωπος ἦν ἐξ ὄρους Εφραιμ ...
readings.en: according to the word of the Lord ... (some 25 added verses)
readings.plain: as the LORD had said. [Here the Greek adds a second account of Jeroboam: his mother Sarira; his fortress and three hundred chariots; his flight to Shishak and marriage to the Egyptian princess Ano; the sickness of their son and Ano's visit to Ahijah; and Shemaiah tearing a new garment into twelve pieces at Shechem.]

why: The supplement is too long and too different in order to be switched into the Hebrew story. Scholars divide over whether it preserves an older form of the story or is a later Jewish retelling; the note on this verse gives both views. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; the bracket only summarizes the Greek.

a: The people walked before the one calf all the way to Dan.
t: A short sentence and longer Greek ones
p: The Hebrew mentions only Dan. The Greek of Codex Vaticanus adds that the people abandoned the LORD's house.

readings.en: and the people went before the one, as far as Dan
readings.plain: The people walked before the one calf all the way to Dan.

readings.orig: ... ἕως Δαν καὶ εἴασαν τὸν οἶκον κυρίου
readings.en: ... as far as Dan, and they abandoned the house of the Lord
readings.plain: The people walked before the one calf all the way to Dan, and they abandoned the house of the LORD.

why: The Hebrew is short and possibly damaged, but it makes sense: the far-off northern shrine drew pilgrims, perhaps in procession. The Greek plus states the consequence the narrator implies: worship at the calves meant leaving the temple in Jerusalem. Some modern translations (NIV, NRSV) also supply 'Bethel' to round out the sentence, as if the people went before one calf at Bethel and the other at Dan. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

a: out of his own heart
p: The reading tradition says Jeroboam devised the month 'from his heart.' The written text has 'by himself' or 'on his own.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (the reading tradition); most translations
readings.en: from his own heart
readings.plain: out of his own heart

readings.en: apart, on his own
readings.plain: on his own

why: The Qere gives the familiar idiom 'devise from one's own heart' (Numbers 16:28; Nehemiah 6:8). The Ketiv, read as 'by himself,' gives much the same meaning: Jeroboam chose the date without any command from God. Either way the narrator's judgment is the same.

a: One of his sons came
p: The Hebrew begins with one son and then says 'they' told their father. The Greek and other versions have 'his sons.'

readings.en: and his son came
readings.plain: One of his sons came

readings.orig: καὶ ἔρχονται οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτοῦ (= וַיָּבֹאוּ בָנָיו)
readings.en: and his sons came
readings.plain: His sons came

why: The Hebrew singular is the harder reading and may simply mean that one son came first and the others joined in the telling. The versions make the verse consistent with its second half and with 13:12. The difference does not change the story.

a: His sons had seen the road the man of God from Judah had gone by
p: The Hebrew says the sons 'had seen' the road. The Greek and other versions say they 'showed him' the road.

readings.en: and his sons had seen
readings.plain: His sons had seen the road the man of God from Judah had gone by

readings.w: Septuagint, Syriac, Targum, Vulgate (a different vowel reading, vayyar'uhu)
readings.en: and his sons showed him
readings.plain: His sons showed him the road the man of God from Judah had gone by

why: Both readings come from nearly the same consonants. 'Showed him' is smoother and many modern translations follow it; the Hebrew 'had seen' also makes sense as background. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

a: Lay my bones next to his bones.
t: 'So that my bones may be saved'
p: The Greek adds a reason: 'so that my bones may be kept safe with his bones.' 2 Kings 23:18 shows what he meant.

readings.en: beside his bones lay my bones
readings.plain: Lay my bones next to his bones.

readings.orig: ... ἵνα σωθῶσι τὰ ὀστᾶ μου μετὰ τῶν ὀστῶν αὐτοῦ
readings.en: ... so that my bones may be saved with his bones
readings.plain: Lay my bones next to his bones, so that my bones may be kept safe with his bones.

why: The Greek plus states what the story implies and what 2 Kings 23:17–18 later shows: when Josiah burned bones on the altar, he spared the man of God's grave, and with it the old prophet's bones. It is probably an explanatory addition, though it could have dropped out of the Hebrew because of the repeated 'his bones.'

a: About that time
t: A chapter the oldest Greek lacks here (14:1–20)
p: Codex Vaticanus has no 14:1–20 here; it tells the story of the sick son inside its supplement after 12:24. See the note on 14:1.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Targum; Vulgate; KJV, NIV, ESV
readings.en: at that time
readings.plain: About that time

readings.en: (14:1–20 is absent)
readings.plain: About that time [The oldest Greek has no 14:1–20 here. It goes straight from the end of chapter 13 to Rehoboam's reign (14:21). A shorter version of this story stands in its supplement at 12:24g–n.]

why: The whole passage is missing, not a phrase, so the switch shows a bracketed summary rather than deleting twenty verses. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew order.

a: Judah did what was evil in the LORD's eyes
p: The Hebrew blames Judah. The Greek and Chronicles blame Rehoboam.

readings.en: and Judah did evil
readings.plain: Judah did what was evil in the LORD's eyes

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus); compare 2 Chronicles 12:14, 'he did evil'
readings.en: and Rehoboam did evil
readings.plain: Rehoboam did what was evil in the LORD's eyes

why: The regnal formula usually says 'he did what was evil,' naming the king, so the Greek reading matches the pattern. That is a reason to suspect it is a correction. The Hebrew 'Judah' fits the rest of the verse, which speaks of 'they' and 'their ancestors.'

a: The one exception was the affair of Uriah the Hittite.
p: The oldest Greek lacks the words about Uriah.

readings.en: except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite
readings.plain: The one exception was the affair of Uriah the Hittite.

readings.en: (the clause is absent)

why: The clause is well attested in Hebrew, and nothing obvious would cause a scribe to drop it. But Kings nowhere else qualifies its praise of David, and many scholars think a later scribe added it as an honest footnote, recalling 2 Samuel 11–12. The Plain English Translation keeps it; the Greek may show an earlier, shorter text.

a: War went on between Rehoboam and Jeroboam as long as he lived.
p: In the middle of Abijam's reign, the Hebrew repeats the note about Rehoboam's war (14:30). Some witnesses read Abijam.

readings.en: there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam
readings.plain: War went on between Rehoboam and Jeroboam as long as he lived.

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac, as reported in the apparatus of BHS
readings.en: there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam
readings.plain: War went on between Abijam and Jeroboam as long as he lived.

readings.en: (the verse is absent)

why: The Hebrew sentence repeats 14:30 almost exactly, and 15:7 then says the same of Abijam. Many think 15:6 is an accidental repetition that a scribe copied from 14:30; the reading 'Abijam' corrects it to fit the context, and the Greek simply lacks it. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew as it stands; 'as long as he lived' then means as long as Rehoboam lived, recalling that the war Abijam inherited began under his father.

a: In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah
p: The Greek has no date by Asa's reign here. Goes with the variants at 16:15 and 16:29.

readings.orig: בִּשְׁנַת עֶשְׂרִים וָשֵׁשׁ שָׁנָה לְאָסָא מֶלֶךְ יְהוּדָה מָלַךְ אֵלָה
readings.en: in the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah reigned
readings.plain: In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah

readings.en: and Ela son of Baasa reigned
readings.plain: Elah

why: See the variant at 16:29. The Greek of these chapters follows its own scheme of dates, and its lack of the Asa synchronisms at 16:8 and 16:15 is part of that scheme. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri
p: The Greek has no date by Asa's reign here. Goes with the variants at 16:8 and 16:29.

readings.orig: בִּשְׁנַת עֶשְׂרִים וָשֶׁבַע שָׁנָה לְאָסָא מֶלֶךְ יְהוּדָה מָלַךְ זִמְרִי
readings.en: in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned
readings.plain: In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri

readings.en: and Zambri reigned
readings.plain: Zimri

why: See the variant at 16:29. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: Tibni died, and Omri reigned.
p: The Greek adds that Tibni's brother Joram died at the same time.

readings.en: and Tibni died, and Omri reigned
readings.plain: Tibni died, and Omri reigned.

readings.en: and Thamni died, and Joram his brother at that time, and Ambri reigned after Thamni
readings.plain: Tibni died, and Joram his brother at that time, and Omri reigned after Tibni.

why: The Hebrew is short and gives no detail of Tibni's death. The Greek plus names a brother, Joram, who is otherwise unknown; it may preserve an old detail from a source, or it may be a later expansion. With no way to test it, the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

a: His son Ahab became king in his place
t: The Greek's extra account of Jehoshaphat (16:28a–h)
p: After this verse the Greek adds eight verses on Jehoshaphat of Judah, a second copy of 22:41–50. See the note on this verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Targum; Vulgate; KJV, NIV, ESV
readings.en: and Ahab his son reigned in his place
readings.plain: His son Ahab became king in his place

readings.en: ... in the eleventh year of Ambri (Omri) ... (eight added verses)
readings.plain: His son Ahab became king in his place. [Here the Greek adds an account of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, dating his accession to Omri's eleventh year and repeating, with small differences, what the Hebrew gives at 22:41–50.]

why: The added verses duplicate material the Hebrew has later, with a different date. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew order; the bracket only summarizes the Greek. The date is part of the Greek's own chronology; see the variant at 16:29.

a: in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah
p: The Hebrew dates Ahab's accession to Asa's 38th year. The Greek dates it to the second year of Jehoshaphat.

readings.orig: בִּשְׁנַת שְׁלֹשִׁים וּשְׁמֹנֶה שָׁנָה לְאָסָא מֶלֶךְ יְהוּדָה
readings.en: in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah
readings.plain: in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah

readings.orig: ἐν ἔτει δευτέρῳ τῷ Ιωσαφατ βασιλεῖ Ιουδα
readings.en: in the second year of Josaphat king of Juda
readings.plain: in the second year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah

why: In the Hebrew, Jehoshaphat comes to the throne in Ahab's fourth year (22:41). The Greek reverses the order: Jehoshaphat begins in Omri's eleventh year (16:28a) and Ahab in Jehoshaphat's second. With the missing synchronisms at 16:8 and 16:15, this is the clearest evidence that the Old Greek carries a different system of dates for the kings. Some scholars think that system is older; most think it is a secondary attempt to solve the problems of the Hebrew figures. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: See the topic on dating the kings, and the note at 16:28.
